## Verse 3:64

> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O People of the Book! Let us come to common terms: that we will worship none but Allah, associate none with Him, nor take one another as lords instead of Allah.” But if they turn away, then say, “Bear witness that we have submitted ˹to Allah alone˺.”

**A COMMON TERM WITH SCRIPTURE COMMUNITIES**

***“Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O People of the Book! Let us come to”*** establishes a common term with scripture communities. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ 'O People of the Book. Let us come to common terms' widens the disputation's close (the surrounding passage) into the Book's most famous interfaith summons. And its instrument's design is the verse's genius. Kalimatin sawa. A word equitable between us. Common terms. The invitation stepping past the contested territories (the natures, the councils, the delegations' doctrines) to the ground every party's own scripture professes. Not compromise's splitting of differences but return to the shared foundation each community's charter already contains. The method of the surrounding passage Ibrahim-answer (past the branches to the root) now issued as standing diplomatic instrument to the People of the Book as such. Najran's Christians, Madinah's Jews. And every scripture-community to history's end. (3:63 — **“then surely Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of the corruptors”**) Today, a common term with scripture communities matters because productive dialogue begins with shared devotion to the one God and refuses both coercion and the elevation of human authorities into lords. Because a common term with scripture communities frames no partner and no human lords, dialogue without the surrender of truth gives a common term with scripture communities its moral consequence. Therefore no partner and no human lords carries a common term with scripture communities into conduct, while dialogue without the surrender of truth preserves a common term with scripture communities by measuring a common term with scripture communities within the verse’s consequences.

**NO PARTNER AND NO HUMAN LORDS**

***“common terms: that we will worship none but Allah, associate none with Him,”*** clarifies the foundation offered to both communities. Worship belongs to Allah alone, so devotion cannot be divided between the Creator and any prophet, saint, institution, or symbol. The next clause excludes association in every form. A community cannot confess one God while directing acts of worship to a created being. The words are common terms because earlier revelation also calls to the one Lord, not because truth is reduced to a negotiated compromise. Ibn ʿAbbās therefore reads the agreement as the declaration that there is no god except Allah. This gives interfaith discussion a clear method. It begins with what revelation holds in common, states the disputed boundary honestly, and refuses both hostility and doctrinal vagueness. Modern dialogue fails when courtesy requires silence about worship, because the verse joins courtesy to an unmistakable confession of divine oneness.

**SUBMISSION STATED AFTER REFUSAL**

***“nor take one another as lords instead of Allah.” But if they turn”*** applies divine oneness to human authority. Taking people as lords includes obeying them when they authorize rebellion against Allah. Ibn ʿAbbās makes that practical meaning explicit: no person may be followed in an act of transgression. Religious learning and communal leadership remain valuable, but neither grants a human being the right to override revelation. The sentence therefore examines every community, including the one issuing the invitation. It does not permit Muslims to condemn priestly domination elsewhere while reproducing unquestionable authority among themselves. The words ***“But if they turn”*** also recognize that a clear invitation may be refused. Refusal does not change the truth or justify coercion. The Messenger ﷺ later placed this verse in his letter to Heraclius, using common worship as the basis of public diplomacy. The next passage shows how argument about inherited identity can obscure that foundation (3:65 — **“O People of the Book! Why do you argue about Abraham,”**).

**DIALOGUE WITHOUT THE SURRENDER OF TRUTH**

***“away, then say, “Bear witness that we have submitted ˹to Allah alone˺.””*** resolves dialogue without the surrender of truth. But if they turn away, then say, 'Attest our surrender to Allah ˹to Allah alone˺' closes the summons with the refused invitation's protocol. And its commanded sentence is the chapter's deepest echo. Bear witness that we are muslims. The disciples' own charter-words (the surrounding passage. Attest our surrender to Allah). The community instructed to answer the scripture-peoples' refusal by declaring itself, in the Gospel-company's exact formula, the standing heirs of what the refusers left. No curse pronounced, no door slammed. A testimony lodged. The common terms remain published, the submitters remain identifiable. And history is left holding the summons still open at this verse's address. Today, dialogue without the surrender of truth matters because productive dialogue begins with shared devotion to the one God and refuses both coercion and the elevation of human authorities into lords. Imagine two communities meeting at a table with one clear foundation. Conversation can continue only while neither side secretly moves the foundation. The comparison makes dialogue without the surrender of truth concrete without reducing submission stated after refusal to the image. At the common term, Ibn ʿAbbās defines agreement as worship of Allah alone, rejection of created partners, refusal to obey people in transgression, and a public declaration of surrender when the invitation is refused.

## Verse 3:154

> Then after distress, He sent down serenity in the form of drowsiness overcoming some of you, while others were disturbed by evil thoughts about Allah—the thoughts of ˹pre-Islamic˺ ignorance. They ask, “Do we have a say in the matter?” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “All matters are destined by Allah.” They conceal in their hearts what they do not reveal to you. They say ˹to themselves˺, “If we had any say in the matter, none of us would have come to die here.” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Even if you were to remain in your homes, those among you who were destined to be killed would have met the same fate.” Through this, Allah tests what is within you and purifies what is in your hearts.
